It stays at the GELU floor when the same words are the grammatical subject ('The video was watched by many people') or the object of a physical-manipulation or possession verb ('moved/pushed/carried/lifted/painted the chair'), and colour terms are its one purely lexical trigger ('bright blue', 'a green scarf', 'a red coat').

Every autumn the county historical society publishes a short bulletin for its members, and this year the editors asked me to write the opening piece. I spent three weekends in the basement of the old courthouse, where the society keeps its boxes, and I want to record what I found there before the details fade from memory.

The building is unremarkable from the street. It was built in 1911, extended twice, and then abandoned for a decade before the county agreed to lease the ground floor to the society for a nominal rent. The heating is unreliable, the lift has been out of service since March, and the only window that opens faces a car park. None of that matters once you are inside the reading room, because the volunteers have done extraordinary work with very little money and almost no publicity.

My own task was modest. I was asked to sort a collection of papers donated by the family of a local schoolteacher, a woman named Margaret Ellis who taught at the grammar school for thirty-one years and kept nearly everything that passed through her hands. There were exercise books, bus tickets, letters from former pupils, a folded map of the estuary, and four photograph albums whose captions had been written in pencil and were badly faded.

Sorting the albums took the better part of a Saturday. The photographs are mostly ordinary: school groups arranged in rows, a summer fete on the recreation ground, a trip to the coast in a chartered bus. What makes them valuable is not the images themselves but the names written beneath them, because Margaret recorded who was present and, in many cases, what became of them afterwards.

In one of the later albums she described the ferry crossing that took her class to the island in 1954, and the annotation runs to nearly a full page. She lists the children in order, notes which ones had never left the county before, and adds a remark about the weather that is unexpectedly funny.

The oldest items in the collection are the exercise books, which are fragile enough that the volunteers now handle them with gloves. Some pages have been repaired with tape that has darkened and cracked, and the archivist would like to have them treated properly, but that too costs money.

The society hopes to digitise the albums next year, but the cost of a decent scanner is beyond its means at present. Anyone who would like to help, or who recognises a name in the photographs, is welcome to write to the address printed on the back page. Small donations are more useful than large promises, as the treasurer likes to say.

I left the courthouse on a grey afternoon with the feeling that I had been allowed to touch something fragile and ordinary at the same time. Margaret Ellis would probably have found the attention puzzling, but I think she would have understood why we keep these things.
